Monotheism vs. the Trinity: Textual and Logical Analysis

Two questions are kept strictly separate (Methodology §5):

  • (a) Textual: Which view does each scripture's own text better support?
  • (b) Logical: Is the Trinity internally coherent, or a contradiction?

The arbiter does not rule on which is divinely true.

1. The two models defined

  • Strict (unitarian) monotheism — God is one in person and essence.
  • Jewish Shema: "Hear O Israel, the LORD our God, the LORD is one" (Deut 6:4).
  • Islamic tawhid: Q 112 ("Say: He is God, One"); Q 4:171, 5:73, 5:116 explicitly reject "three" and reject Jesus-as-God; associating partners (shirk) is the gravest sin.
  • Trinitarian monotheism — one God in essence (ousia) eternally existing as three persons (hypostaseis): Father, Son, Spirit; the Son incarnate in Jesus. This is not tritheism (three gods) and not modalism (one person in three modes) — both were declared heresies.

2. The textual question — what do the sources say?

Qur'an

Unambiguous and explicit for strict monotheism. The Qur'an directly addresses and rejects the Trinity and the deity of Christ (Q 4:171, 5:72–75, 5:116). On the text's own terms there is no internal tension: strict monotheism is stated outright.

Note: Q 5:116 frames a "Trinity" as God, Jesus, and Mary. Scholars dispute whether this (i) misstates orthodox Trinitarianism, (ii) targets a real heterodox/Marian sect, or (iii) is rhetorical. This is itself a contested data point and is flagged, not resolved.

Bible

There is no single verse that states the doctrine of the Trinity in creedal form (and the clearest would-be proof-text, the Comma Johanneum 1 John 5:7, is not original — see Bible Transmission). The Trinitarian case is built cumulatively:

  • Strict-monotheism / unitarian-leaning data: Deut 6:4; Isa 45:5; Mark 12:29 (Jesus affirms the Shema); John 17:3; 1 Cor 8:6; "the Father is greater than I" (John 14:28); Jesus prays to God; 1 Tim 2:5.
  • High-Christology / Trinitarian data: John 1:1, 1:14; John 8:58 ("before Abraham was, I am"); John 10:30; John 20:28 ("My Lord and my God"); Phil 2:6–11; Col 1:15–20, 2:9; Heb 1; Matt 28:19 (triadic baptismal formula); 2 Cor 13:14; the Spirit as personal and divine (Acts 5:3–4).

So the biblical text is genuinely bivalent: it contains both strongly monotheistic and strongly high-Christological strands. The Trinity is a later doctrinal synthesis that attempts to hold both strands together without collapsing into tritheism or denying Jesus' deity.

Historical development (the academic record)

  • Devotion to Jesus as in some sense divine is very early — Hurtado (Lord Jesus Christ) and Bauckham (Jesus and the God of Israel) argue for a high "Christology of divine identity" within the first two decades, inside a Jewish monotheistic frame.
  • Ehrman (How Jesus Became God) argues the exalted status escalated over time from a lower starting point.
  • The formal doctrine was hammered out against rival models: Arianism (Son created/subordinate) → Nicaea 325 (homoousios, "same essence") → Constantinople 381 (full deity of the Spirit) → Chalcedon 451 (two natures of Christ). These councils defined and regulated the doctrine; the genetic fallacy (Methodology §4) forbids inferring from "defined in 325" that "the underlying belief was absent in 30–100" — that has to be argued from the texts, where the evidence is mixed and early-contested.

3. The logical question — is the Trinity coherent?

The Islamic / unitarian objection

  • It looks like a contradiction: God is one and three.
  • It looks like shirk: associating a created/human being with God.
  • Incarnation seems to impose creaturely limits (hunger, death, ignorance — Mark 13:32) on the immutable, transcendent God.

The Trinitarian reply

  • The classic formula avoids formal contradiction by qualifying the terms: God is one in essence and three in person — "one" and "three" are predicated of different things, so it is not "1=3."
  • Models: Latin/Augustinian (one divine substance, three subsistent relations), Social Trinitarianism (three centers of consciousness in perfect unity of essence/will), relative-identity approaches (Geach/van Inwagen). Philosophers (W. L. Craig, R. Swinburne, P. van Inwagen, B. Leftow) defend coherence; critics (and many Muslim philosophers, classically the kalam tradition) argue every model either slides into tritheism or modalism.
  • All analogies (water states, sun/light/heat, etc.) are admitted by careful theologians to be imperfect and are not the doctrine itself.

Arbiter note on the logic

  • "Triune" is not a strict logical contradiction as stated, because the predicates are indexed to different categories (essence vs. person). A bare "1 = 3" objection fails.
  • However, the doctrine is not transparently self-evident either: its coherence depends on technical metaphysical machinery (essence/person, perichoresis, the homoousion) that is not given in the texts and is itself internally contested among Trinitarian philosophers.
  • Strict monotheism (tawhid / unitarianism) has the advantage of logical simplicity and immediacy: it requires no special apparatus to state without contradiction.

Arbiter verdict — monotheism vs. Trinity

Present.

  • Islamic/unitarian: the Qur'an states strict monotheism outright; the Bible's clearest Trinity proof-text is a spurious insertion; the Trinity is a post-biblical synthesis and is logically strained.
  • Christian: the NT contains undeniable high-Christological and triadic data; the Trinity is the best synthesis of all the biblical strands; and, properly stated, it is not a formal contradiction.

Weigh.

  • Textual fit, Qur'an → tawhid: very strong — explicit and internally consistent.
  • Textual fit, Bible → Trinity: partial — the Trinity is the synthesizing doctrine of a genuinely two-stranded text; it is inferred and developed, not stated; the strongest single proof-text is not original.
  • Textual fit, Bible → strict unitarianism: also partial — it must explain away the high-Christology strand, which is early and real.
  • Logical coherence: strict monotheism is simpler and not contradictory; the Trinity is not formally contradictory but is metaphysically heavy and internally contested.

Judge.

  • On "which view does each scripture's own text most directly support?": the Qur'an unambiguously supports strict monotheism (clear win on its own text). The Bible does not unambiguously support either in stated form — it supports a cumulative Trinitarian reading better than a strict-unitarian one only because of the early high-Christology strand, while not stating the creedal doctrine itself. So: Qur'an → strict monotheism, decisively on the text; Bible → Trinity, by synthesis, not by explicit statement.
  • On "is the Trinity logically incoherent?": the strong charge (it is a flat contradiction) fails; the weaker charge (it is not self-evident and rests on contested metaphysics absent from the texts) succeeds.
  • The honest arbiter result: this section is not symmetric with the transmission sections. Here the Qur'an's position is textually cleaner, while the Bible's position is textually richer but doctrinally constructed. Which one counts as a virtue depends on a prior, non-historical assumption about whether revelation should be simple or developed — and that the arbiter cannot decide (Methodology §5).
